newsitem.title: USA: Pfizer says calcium-channel blockers safe.
newsitem.headline: Pfizer says calcium-channel blockers safe.

text.p: Pfizer Inc said Wednesday that studies conducted by scientists at two cardiovascular research centers show that calcium-channel blockers are safe to use.
Calcium-channel blockers are drugs commonly used to treat high blood pressure and heart disease.
The studies cited by Pfizer, and presented Wednesday to the American Heart Association meeting in New Orleans, involved data from the Framingham Heart Study and a study at the Cleveland Clinic.

Pfizer said that in a review of calcium channel blocker use among patients enrolled in the Framingham Heart Study, researchers reported that "we found no evidence of increased mortality risk in hypertensive CCB patients." The study also showed the finding was true regardless of whether patients had an underlying coronary disease, the company said.

The Framingham Heart Study, instituted by the National Heart, Lung and Blood Institute of the National Institutes of Health, is an ongoing scientific inquiry into the development and progression of heart disease.
The other study presented at the conference was conducted by researchers at Cleveland Clinic.

That review showed that records from more than 5,100 "surgical patients showed no increased risk of excessive bleeding" when calcium channel blockers were used, the company said. An earlier paper on the issue had raised questions about possible excessive bleeding based on data from 112 patients, it said.
"The results from the Cleveland Clinic are striking because of the large number of patients examined," Pfizer Senior Vice President of Medical Affairs Dr. Roger Sachs said in a statement.
"Further, the patients in the group at greatest risk of bleeding had better outcomes when treated with CCBs compared with patients not treated with CCBs."

Dr. Milton Packer of Columbia-Presbyterian Medical Center said in a statement that the "data presented against calcium-channel blockers does not meet rigorous scientific standards of evidence. In fact, if the same standards of evidence were used, similar concerns could be raised for many anti-hypertensives which are known to be safe."

The Lancet report was based on research conducted by Dr. Marco Pahor of the University of Tennessee in Memphis who looked at the health records of more than 5,000 men and women over the age of 70 in the United States. Of them, 451 had been using calcium-channel blockers.
Those who used calcium channel blockers were 70 percent more likely to develop cancer, and the more drugs they took, the higher their risk, Pahor's group wrote in the Lancet.
Nevertheless, Pahor said at the time that people should not stop taking the drugs, saying the evidence from a single study is not sufficient to recommend withdrawal of the treatment.
